sections.heading: How to generate a LinkedIn headline
sections.body:
Open the [LinkedIn headline generator](https://linkedin-headline.lazur.app/) in your browser. Describe your work in the first box, add who you help or want to impress if you like, and run it. You will see five options. Pick one, copy it, and paste it into the headline field of your LinkedIn profile.

1. Open [the generator](https://linkedin-headline.lazur.app/).
2. Write what you do in plain words, such as your job title and your main skill.
3. Optionally add who you help or want to impress, such as hiring managers in a field or clients in a city.
4. Run the generator and read all five options.
5. Copy the one that sounds most like you, then paste it into your profile.

**Start with the job title.** Recruiters and clients search by role, so the title you want to be found for should come early in the headline you choose.

sections.heading: What to type in the boxes
sections.body:
The first box asks what you do. Write it the way you would explain your work to a stranger at a conference: a job title, the two or three skills you use most, and one thing you are known for. A short, specific description gives the tool something to work with. For example, 'Backend developer, Python and PostgreSQL, payment systems' is enough.

The second box is optional. Use it when you know who should notice you, such as hiring managers for data roles, founders who need a designer, or buyers in one industry. The headlines then speak to that reader. Leave it empty if you want general options that fit many readers.

Do not paste a long life story. The headlines can only be as specific as your input. If you type only 'hard worker', the options will be vague. Add a skill or a result you can prove, such as a project you shipped or a team you led, and only if it is true.

sections.heading: What the five options look like
sections.body:
The tool returns five headlines, and each one is under 220 characters. Each option says what you do and for whom. The options are kept apart so you can copy one at a time. You get no numbering, no labels and no note before or after the list, so the text you copy is the headline itself.

Read all five before you choose. Pick the one that sounds like you at your best, in plain words. If none of them fits, change the first box and run the tool again. A new description often gives you five different angles on the same work, so try two or three versions before you decide.

You can also compare the options against each other. One may lead with the job title, another with a skill, and a third with the people you serve. Notice which pattern feels most true and keep that one.

sections.heading: Check the headline before you paste it
sections.body:
A headline is a short summary, so read each option the way a stranger would. Ask three questions. Do the first few words name the job you want to be found for? Can you back up every claim in an interview? Does it sound like you talking, not like an advertisement?

Remove filler words if they do not fit. The tool is set to avoid words such as 'passionate' or 'guru', and you should cut similar words yourself. They are easy to write and tell the reader very little. Replace them with a skill or a result you can explain.

**The tool writes from what you typed.** It does not check your work history or your résumé, so the facts in the final headline are your responsibility. Edit any option by hand if a word is off.

sections.heading: Free use, no sign-up, and one tip
sections.body:
The generator is free and needs no account. You get 3 runs a day. After those, you can leave an email for 3 more runs. Results can be copied with one click, so you do not need to retype them.

If you write posts and messages every day on a Mac, [Lazur](https://www.lazur.app/) does this kind of work in any app: hold two keys, talk, and the text appears where your cursor is.

pages.title: LinkedIn Headline Generator From Resume | Lazur
pages.description: Turn your resume into a LinkedIn headline. Copy your job title and top skills into the generator, then pick one of five free options. No sign-up needed.
pages.claim: Copy the job title, top skills and one result from your resume into the generator. It writes five LinkedIn headlines, each under 220 characters, that say what you do and for whom. Free, no account needed.

sections.heading: Pick the parts of your resume to copy
sections.body:
Your resume is long, but a headline has room for only a few words. Open your resume and find three things: the job title you want next, the two or three skills that show up most in your work, and one result you can prove. Leave the rest for now. Your education dates, your full job history and your old objective statement do not belong in a headline.

Type those three things into the first box of the [generator](https://linkedin-headline.lazur.app/) as plain words. For example: 'Product manager, B2B software, roadmap planning, pricing work, launched two product lines.' Use only results that your resume actually states, and copy the wording as it is written there, so the headline matches the document a recruiter will read next.

sections.heading: Use the job you want, not only the job you have
sections.body:
Many resumes name the job you hold now. A headline works better when it names the job people search for. If your resume says 'Customer support associate' but you are aiming for a customer success role, write the target title in the first box and keep the support work as proof.

Use the optional second box to say who should notice you, such as 'hiring managers at software companies' or 'clients who need a bookkeeper for small firms'. The options then speak to that reader, which matters more than adding extra buzzwords.

If your resume covers several kinds of work, pick the direction you want next and leave out the rest. A headline that tries to name every past job is hard to read, and it does not tell a recruiter which search to match.

sections.heading: Check each option against the resume
sections.body:
Each option should match what your resume can back up. Take each headline and check every claim against a line in your resume. If a headline says 'led a team' and your resume shows no team, cut that part. If it names a tool you used once in a class, you may want to remove it too.

1. Do the first few words name a job someone would search for?
2. Does every skill appear somewhere in your real work?
3. Could you explain the proof in an interview without notes?

Keep the option that passes all three checks. Edit it by hand if one word is off. The tool gives you a strong start, but you are the one who knows the facts, so the final wording is yours.

sections.heading: Paste it into your profile and update it later
sections.body:
Copy the headline you chose and paste it into the headline field on your LinkedIn profile. Keep the job title at the front after any edit, because that is the part a search is most likely to match. Then check that your about section and your experience entries tell the same story, so the headline is backed by the rest of the page.

When your resume changes, such as after a new job, a promotion or a finished certificate, run the generator again with the new facts. Your headline should follow your work. A headline that stays the same for years can make a new skill invisible to the people who search for it.

faq.q: What is a catchy headline for LinkedIn?
faq.a: A catchy LinkedIn headline names the job you want and one specific skill or result, in plain words. The generator writes five options in that pattern, each under 220 characters, so you can compare them side by side. Avoid vague praise such as 'passionate' or 'guru', because those words tell the reader nothing they can check.

faq.q: What is a good headline for a LinkedIn profile for an IT professional?
faq.a: A good IT headline names your role and your main technology, such as 'Systems administrator, Windows and Microsoft 365, cloud migration'. Add the environment you support if it matters to the reader. Type your role and tools into the generator, then pick the option that sounds like something you could say in a job interview.

faq.q: Do I need to paste my whole resume into the generator?
faq.a: No. The generator works from the short description you type, so you only need the job title, the main skills and one result. A short, specific description is enough for the tool to write from, and it keeps the options focused on what matters to a reader.

pages.title: LinkedIn Headline Generator for Students | Lazur
pages.description: Write a LinkedIn headline as a student. Name your field, the role you want and what you have built or studied, then pick from five free options.
pages.claim: Type your field, the role you want, and one thing you have built or studied. The generator writes five LinkedIn headlines, each under 220 characters. Free, no account needed.

sections.heading: What a student headline needs
sections.body:
A student headline has no long job history to lean on, so it needs a different hook. Lead with the field and the role you want, not the school name. A headline such as 'Computer science student seeking software engineering internships' tells a recruiter what you are after in one line. The school name can go in your education section, where it already has room.

A strong student headline usually has three parts: your field, the role you are after, and one proof point, such as a project, a course or a club you ran. Keep the list short. Three parts fit inside 220 characters with room to spare, and a long list of courses makes the headline hard to scan.

sections.heading: Fill in the generator for your situation
sections.body:
Open the [LinkedIn headline generator](https://linkedin-headline.lazur.app/) and describe your work in the first box. Use plain words, such as 'Second-year nursing student, placement experience, interested in community health roles'. Then use the optional second box for who should notice you, such as 'hiring managers for summer internships'.

1. Write your field and your year, such as 'Marketing student, final year'.
2. Name the role you want, such as 'marketing assistant' or 'research intern'.
3. Add one thing you have made or done, such as a campaign you ran for a club.
4. Run the generator and compare the five options.

If you have done no paid work in your field yet, say so in your own words in the first box. The options will still name the role and the field, and you can add the proof point you do have, such as a class project.

sections.heading: Choose a headline you can defend
sections.body:
Recruiters who read a student headline often ask one simple question: can this person do the work? Pick the option that gives an honest answer. If an option says 'expert in data analysis' and you have finished one course, change it to 'data analysis coursework' or cut the word 'expert'. An honest headline holds up better in an interview than an impressive one you cannot explain.

Words such as 'passionate', 'driven' and 'guru' take up space without proof. Replace them with a skill you can show: a tool you have used, a project you finished, or a role you held. Read the final choice out loud. If it sounds like an advertisement, rewrite it the way you would talk about your work to a friend.

sections.heading: Put the headline on your profile
sections.body:
Copy the headline you chose and paste it into the headline field on your LinkedIn profile. Then check that the rest of your profile matches it. Your about section and your project entries should back up the skills in the headline. A headline that promises data analysis should be followed by a project that shows it.

When you finish a course, join a club or ship a project, run the generator again with the new facts. Students change quickly, and a headline written last year can undersell you now.

faq.q: What should my LinkedIn headline be if I am a student?
faq.a: Name your field and the role you want, then add one proof point such as a project or a course. For example: 'Computer science student seeking software engineering internships, built a campus app.' The generator writes five options in this pattern, each under 220 characters, so you can pick the one that is true for you.

faq.q: What are headline examples for students?
faq.a: Good student headlines state a field, a target role and a proof point. Examples include 'Nursing student, placement experience, targeting community health roles' or 'Finance student and Excel modeler, seeking summer analyst internships'. Use the generator with your own field so the wording matches what you actually do, not a copied example.

faq.q: Is it okay to say I am a student in my headline?
faq.a: Yes. Saying you are a student is accurate and common, and it tells recruiters where you are on your path. Put the role you want first so the headline is searchable, then name your studies. You can remove the student label from any option if you would rather lead with the field alone.

The tool is an AI writer for one job: LinkedIn headlines. It runs on Google Gemini on Lazur's servers. You type what you do, optionally add who you help or want to impress, and the tool returns five headlines. Each one is under 220 characters and says what you do and for whom.

The answer usually appears in about 1 to 3 seconds. The output has no numbering, no labels and no extra text before or after the list, so each option is a headline you can read and copy on its own.

sections.heading: What to type
sections.body:
Use two inputs. The first is required: what you do. Write a job title and two or three skills, such as 'Backend developer, Python and PostgreSQL, payment systems'. The second is optional: who you help or want to impress, such as 'founders who need a fast API'.

Short and specific works best. A long life story gives the tool more to sort through, and the headlines can come out vague. You do not need to ask for a tone. The tool is set to avoid words such as 'passionate' or 'guru', and it writes in plain, specific language by default.

If you are a freelancer, name the work you do for clients. If you are employed, name your current role and the team you work with. The more concrete the first box, the easier it is to choose a headline that sounds like you.

sections.heading: Pick and check your headline
sections.body:
Read all five options, then choose one you could explain in an interview. Check that the first words name the role someone would search for. Check that each skill appears in your real work, and that the claim is true.

1. Read all five options out loud.
2. Cross out any claim you cannot back up.
3. Copy the one that fits, then paste it into your LinkedIn headline field.

If none fits, change the first box with new words and run the tool again. A new description often gives you five new options, so try two or three versions before you decide. Keep the one that sounds most like how you talk about your work.

The tool is free and needs no account. You get 3 runs a day. After those, you can leave an email for 3 more runs. Results can be copied with one click, so you do not need to retype them.

If you use up your runs for the day, you can come back the next day, or use the three extra runs after you leave an email. Nothing else is needed to use the tool.

sections.heading: Make the rest of your profile match
sections.body:
A headline gets someone to click. Your about section and your experience decide whether they stay. Use the headline as a promise and make sure the rest of your profile backs it up. If the headline names a skill, the about section should show that skill in use, with one example you can point to.

Revisit the headline when your work changes. A new role, a new skill or a finished project is a good reason to run the tool again and pick a fresh option.

faq.q: How do I create a strong LinkedIn headline?
faq.a: Start with the job title you want, add one or two skills you use, and end with a proof point that is true. The tool writes five options in that pattern, each under 220 characters. Read them out loud, cut any claim you cannot back up, and keep the one that sounds most like you.

faq.q: Can ChatGPT write my LinkedIn profile?
faq.a: Other AI tools can write LinkedIn text, but this tool is built for one thing: headlines. You describe what you do, and it returns five headlines, each under 220 characters, that name the work and the reader. Use it for the headline, then write the rest of your profile yourself so it stays true to your experience.

faq.q: Is the LinkedIn headline generator free?
faq.a: Yes. You get 3 runs a day with no account needed. After those, you can leave an email for 3 more runs. Results can be copied with one click. The tool is free to use and does not require a LinkedIn login.
